The N.I.C.E. process keeps a project anchored to a real situation instead of a favourite product. Students define the need, investigate what already exists, create and communicate alternatives, build and test a prototype, evaluate evidence, and use what they learned to begin another cycle.

<ol class="ter-design-cycle" aria-label="N.I.C.E. design process">
  <li>Needs</li>
  <li>Inquiry</li>
  <li>Create</li>
  <li>Evaluate</li>
  <li>Repeat</li>
</ol>

## Free online research resources

Use [Instructables](https://www.instructables.com/) and [Hackaday.io](https://hackaday.io/projects) for documented builds, [Google Patents](https://patents.google.com/) for mechanism and product-history research, and [Cambridge Inclusive Design](https://www-edc.eng.cam.ac.uk/research/inclusive-design) for designing around varied users. These are investigation sources, not permission to copy. The [full free-resource directory](../resources/index.qmd) explains access, licence, attribution, and verification checks.

## Ontario curriculum design process

The same cycle supports technological problem solving across Ontario secondary school technology courses: identify a need, investigate, develop and communicate alternatives, plan and create, test against criteria and constraints, evaluate evidence, and improve the response.

::: {.ter-curriculum-relevance}
**Ontario curriculum relevance:** Useful for **TIJ1O Exploring Technologies** and transferable to **TDJ2O Technological Design**, senior TDJ courses, and other Ontario Technological Education projects that require needs analysis, technological problem solving, engineering design, communication, prototyping, feedback, and iteration.
:::
